hops.afterHeading: The typical response: a burst at each end
hops.title: Feeling paper through a ballpoint pen
hops.text: Rest a fingertip on a sheet of printer paper, hold it perfectly still, and try to judge its texture. In lab tests with abrasive surfaces, differences in roughness became much harder to feel without sliding once the grains were smaller than about 100 micrometers, because a held press supplies no vibration. Now drag the tip of a capped ballpoint pen across the paper, then across your sleeve and the desk. Plastic has no nerves, yet each surface comes through clearly. Studies with handheld probes find that roughness felt this way is close to what the bare finger reports, carried up the barrel as vibration.

sources.citation: Hollins M, Risner SR (2000). Evidence for the duplex theory of tactile texture perception. Percept. Psychophys. 62(4):695-705.
Yoshioka T, Bensmaia SJ, Craig JC, Hsiao SS (2007). Texture perception through direct and indirect touch. Somatosens. Mot. Res. 24(1-2):53-70.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A hand lightly dragging a capped ballpoint pen across a denim sleeve and blank paper on a wooden desk.
image.caption: A still fingertip loses fine texture; a sliding pen carries it to your hand as vibration.

hops.afterHeading: Where force becomes current: Piezo2 in the axon
hops.title: Two patients born without working PIEZO2
hops.text: In 2016 a team at the National Institutes of Health described two patients, first seen at ages 18 and 8, born with inactivating variants in the PIEZO2 gene. Asked whether a 150 hertz vibration on the hairless skin of the hand was on or off, healthy volunteers were right 98 percent of the time. The patients managed 40 percent, no better than chance. They showed reduced vibration sensitivity on the forearm as well, and with eyes closed they could not walk and had profoundly impaired joint-position sense. Yet both sensed warmth and coolness much like controls, and both detected slow brushing on the forearm every time.

sources.citation: Chesler AT et al. (2016). The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation. N. Engl. J. Med. 375(14):1355-1364.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small metal vibrating probe on a wooden table beside a steaming teacup and an ice cube on a saucer.
image.caption: Both patients had severely impaired vibration and joint sense but still felt warmth and coolness much like controls.

hops.afterHeading: Vibration in the brain and in the wild
hops.title: How planthoppers led a biologist to elephant feet
hops.text: Before she studied elephants, biologist Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell spent hours in a soundproof chamber in Hawaii watching planthoppers, small insects that send calls through plant stems. She saw them call, freeze, press down on the stem and sometimes lift a leg. In 1992, at a watering hole in Namibia's Etosha National Park, she watched a herd of African elephants freeze with ears flat, rise onto their toes and sometimes raise one foot. Later studies of Asian elephants measured rumbles and stomps traveling through the ground at around 20 hertz, and found clusters of Pacinian corpuscles in their feet. Whether those corpuscles do the listening is still a proposal.

sources.citation: White T (2007). Caller ID in the wild: Elephants hear underground. Stanford Medicine News Center.
Ernst C (2007). Understanding Elephants. Malamalama, University of Hawaii System 32(2).
O'Connell-Rodwell CE, Arnason BT, Hart LA (2000). Seismic properties of Asian elephant vocalizations and locomotion. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 108(6):3066-3072.

audio.title: A spicy tingle, a probing bill and the job of fingerprints
audio.transcript:
Rapidly adapting touch afferents care about change, and that shows up in some odd places: a bowl of noodles, a muddy beach, and the tips of your own fingers.

Start with dinner. Sichuan pepper does not burn the way a chili does. It makes your lips tingle, almost buzz. In two thousand thirteen, Nobuhiro Hagura and colleagues at University College London asked what frequency that buzz feels like. They put Sichuan pepper on volunteers' lower lips, then asked again and again which felt faster: the tingle on the lip or a mechanical vibration on the right index finger. From those answers the researchers worked out the matching frequency, and it came out consistently at about fifty hertz. That is within the range of the R A one afferents linked to Meissner corpuscles, the touch pathway associated with flutter. Then came the clever part. After sustained mechanical vibration applied to the lips, the pepper's tingle felt lower in frequency. Nothing in the peppercorn is shaking, yet your lips report a vibration that is not there. From that frequency shift, the researchers inferred that the spice taps into a touch pathway shared with mechanical vibration.

Next, a shorebird. The red knot feeds on hard-shelled clams buried deep in wet sand, out of sight. In a study published in nineteen ninety-eight, Theunis Piersma and colleagues trained red knots to probe one bucket of wet sand at a time and report whether it held a buried object by choosing one of two feeders. Some buckets hid clams. Then the team slipped in buckets hiding plain stones. The birds detected the stones too, which made smell, taste and the movements of live clams unlikely explanations. In dry sand, the birds could no longer tell which buckets held clams. The authors' best explanation is water pressure. Each quick probe of the bill pushes on the water between the sand grains, and a buried solid object disturbs that pressure pattern. The bill tip is packed with Herbst corpuscles, the bird counterpart of the Pacinian corpuscle, sitting in tiny pits in the bone, and the authors inferred that these pick up the change. Kiwis and ibises have similar touch-sensitive bill tips, and fossils suggest finding hidden prey by touch at a distance dates back to the Cretaceous.

Last, your fingerprints. Ask around and most people will say the ridges are there for grip, like the tread on a tire. In two thousand nine, Peter Warman and Roland Ennos pressed fingertips against acrylic glass in a testing machine. The skin behaved more like rubber than like a hard solid, and the ridges reduced the area of skin actually touching the glass. For a rubbery material, less contact means less friction, so the authors concluded that fingerprints are unlikely to increase grip on smooth surfaces like that one. In a study published that same year, another team slid an artificial fingertip with parallel ridges across finely textured glass. Sliding perpendicular to the ridges, rather than along them, emphasized pressure fluctuations near one frequency: the sliding speed divided by the ridge spacing. For a real fingertip with ridges about half a millimeter apart, sliding perpendicular to those ridges at ten to fifteen centimeters a second over a fine texture, the researchers estimated two hundred to three hundred hertz, close to where human Pacinian afferents are most sensitive. So fingerprints may work as a filter, shaping texture into the kind of signal your change detectors read best.

A sliding fingertip makes vibrations, a probing bill may read pressure changes, and a spice can make your lips feel a vibration that is not there. All three point to touch pathways built to signal movement and change.
